finding.claim: The /settings/email POST endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid=None. Missing authentication on a state-changing account operation. An anonymous attacker can trigger an email change, and if set_email treats a None uid as a match or a lookup by null, it could modify unowned or arbitrary records. It also gives an unauthenticated write path and is likely a copy-paste decorator mistake next to the correct login_required on /settings/password.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid') which is None for anonymous users, and does not abort
set_email(None, ...) is called with no authorization check

finding.guards_checked: login_required is not used on this route (it is used on /settings/password, line 42). No other auth, ownership, or CSRF check exists in the file. login_optional never aborts. No CSRF protection is configured on the Flask app, so state-changing POSTs are also CSRF-exposed for authenticated users. set_email is a stub so the impact of a None uid depends on the real implementation.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts; no ownership or CSRF check; the only abort is in login_required, which is not applied here)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password, which uses login_required at routes.py:42; set_email is only a stub (routes.py:48), so the real impact of a None uid is unknown.
